summary: Geoffrey Barstow specializes in Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies. He studied at Hampshire College, Kathmandu University, and under Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche, earning his PhD from the University of Virginia before becoming assistant professor of religious studies at Oregon State University (~2014).

Geoffrey Goble is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. He earned an MA at the University of Virginia and a PhD at Indiana University Bloomington, later serving as assistant professor of religious studies at the University of Oklahoma (2016).

Geoffrey Samuel works in religious studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He studied at Oxford and Cambridge under Edmund Leach, Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah, and Peter J. Wilson. He held posts at Otago, Lancaster, and Newcastle (1978–2004), later becoming Emeritus Professor at Cardiff University (2014).

Georg August Wallin was a Finnish scholar of linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Katedralskolan i Åbo and the University of Helsinki (~1829–1836), where he later held an academic post from circa 1851 to 1852.

Georg Buddruss was a scholar of Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned his doctorate under Paul Thieme at Goethe University Frankfurt (~1950–1954), studied at Tübingen, and was professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz from 1963 to 1995.

Georg Bühler was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Theodor Benfey at Göttingen. He held posts at Elphinstone College and Bombay Presidency (1863–1880), followed by the chair of Indian philology and archaeology at the University of Vienna from 1880.
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg was a philosopher and academic. He studied at the University of Göttingen from circa 1763 to 1769 and subsequently held a post there from circa 1770 until 1799.

Georg Curtius was a German linguist who studied at Bonn and Berlin under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, Christian Lassen, and Franz Bopp. After completing his doctorate and habilitation in Berlin, he served as a professor at the University of Leipzig from 1862 to 1885.

Georg Ebers was an Egyptologist and linguist who studied at Göttingen, Berlin, and Jena under Karl Richard Lepsius and August Boeckh. He held academic posts at the University of Jena (1869–1870) and the University of Leipzig (1870–1889).

Georg Forster was a scholar of Indology and natural history who attended Saint Peter's School. He served as professor of natural history at Collegium Carolinum (1779) and Vilnius University (1784–1787), and was later university librarian and professor at Mainz (~1788–1792).

Georg Freytag was an Orientalist and linguist. He studied at the University of Göttingen and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy in Paris, subsequently serving as repetent at Göttingen (1811–1813) and as professor of Oriental languages at the University of Bonn (1819–1861).

Georg Friedrich Grotefend was a scholar of linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne, Thomas Christian Tychsen, and Arnold Heeren, later serving as prorector at Lessing-Gymnasium (1803) and director of Ratsgymnasium Hannover (1821–1849).
Georg Grimm was a specialist in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He lectured on Buddhism at the University of Munich and founded the Altbuddhistische Gemeinde in 1921.

Georg Heinrich Bernstein was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Jena, Leipzig, Göttingen, and under Franz Bopp, holding positions as Privatdozent at Jena (1811), extraordinary professor at Berlin (1812), and ordinary professor at the University of Breslau (1820).

Georg Heinrich Ferdinand Nesselmann worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned his doctorate at the University of Königsberg under Peter von Bohlen, where he successively served as Privatdozent (1838), extraordinary professor (1843), and ordinary professor (1859).

Georg Huth was an Indologist and Tibetologist who studied at Berlin, Kiel, and Leipzig under Ernst Windisch, Albrecht Weber, and others. He served as Privatdozent for Tibetan and Mongolian at Berlin (1891) and worked at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin (~1902–1906).

Georg Jacob was an Orientalist who completed his PhD at Leipzig under Fleischer after studying at Erlangen, Breslau, and Strasbourg. He held professorships in Semitic languages at Erlangen (1901–1909) and in Islamic and Semitic philology at Kiel (1911–1929).

Georg Kaibel was a scholar of linguistics, history, and archaeology. During his career, he held posts at the University of Rostock (~1879–1882), University of Greifswald (~1882–1883), University of Breslau (~1883–1886), and the University of Göttingen (~1897–1901).

Georg Ludolf Dissen was a German classicist and linguist. He completed his studies at the University of Göttingen (~1804–1807) and subsequently held academic posts at the University of Marburg (~1812–1813) and the University of Göttingen (~1813–1837).

Georg Martin Dursch was an Indologist and theologian. He earned a doctorate at the University of Tübingen, studied Sanskrit in Paris under Antoine-Léonard Chézy (~1826–1829), and served as a professor at the Johann-Vanotti-Gymnasium in Ehingen starting in 1828.
